_note: Deep-time visuals, kept apart from the records so that adding one never edits a record. scenes: which schematic effect a record's animation plays (km comes from the record where it states a size). labels: names drawn on the moving continents, in millions of years ago, with approximate dates. marks: mass extinctions and ice ages on the time bar. film: the guided film; each caption states only what the record named beside it says.

marks.label: Antarctic ice sheet, from about 34 million years ago

film.title: A billion years of Earth
film.blurb: One continuous shot of the moving continents, about three minutes long, drawn from the records.
film.credit: Land and sea floor: PALEOMAP PaleoDEMs (Scotese and Wright 2018). Older plate motion: MERDITH2021. Fossils: Paleobiology Database. Sea level: Spratt and Lisiecki 2016. Ice sheets: PaleoMIST 1.0. Impact, eruption and plant effects are schematic. Temperature, CO₂ and day length: estimates, sources in About.
film.end: Every chapter comes from a record in this atlas. Open any pin to read it and its sources.

chapters.title: Rodinia
chapters.caption: A billion years ago, mountain building joins several continents into the supercontinent Rodinia.

chapters.title: Snowball Earth
chapters.caption: About 717 million years ago the Sturtian glaciation begins, one of the ice ages called Snowball Earth. A second, the Marinoan, ends about 635 million years ago.

chapters.title: The first large life
chapters.caption: From about 571 million years ago, large soft-bodied Ediacaran organisms spread through the oceans.

chapters.title: Animals
chapters.caption: From about 539 million years ago, almost every major animal body plan appears in the fossil record within some 20 to 30 million years.

chapters.title: Plants reach land
chapters.caption: Microscopic spores about 480 million years old are the oldest evidence of plants on land.

chapters.title: Ice and extinction
chapters.caption: About 445 million years ago comes a mass extinction: one study of brachiopods counts 69% of genera lost.

chapters.title: Dying seas
chapters.caption: About 372 million years ago, oceanic anoxia accompanies massive losses of marine life.

chapters.title: Pangaea
chapters.caption: Gondwana and Laurussia converge as the Rheic Ocean closes, joining the continents into the supercontinent Pangaea.

chapters.title: The worst extinction
chapters.caption: About 251.9 million years ago, most marine species die within roughly 60,000 years, most likely set off by Siberian Traps magmatism.

chapters.title: Pangaea breaks apart
chapters.caption: From about 201 million years ago the Central Atlantic opens, Laurasia and Gondwana separate, and the South Atlantic unzips.

chapters.title: The end of the dinosaurs
chapters.caption: About 66.04 million years ago an asteroid roughly 10 km wide strikes the shallow sea off Yucatán, triggering a mass extinction.

chapters.title: India meets Asia
chapters.caption: India, moving north, collides with Asia, raising the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau. The date is disputed: about 59 to 40 million years ago.

chapters.title: Antarctica freezes
chapters.caption: Around 34 million years ago Earth shifts from a largely ice-free greenhouse to an icehouse, with the first major glaciation of Antarctica.

chapters.title: Our species
chapters.caption: Around 300,000 years ago our species, Homo sapiens, is taking shape in Africa.

chapters.title: The last ice age
chapters.caption: The Last Glacial Maximum, about 26,500 to 19,000 years ago, marks the peak of the continental ice sheets, with sea level about 130 metres lower. Then the ice melts back.
